Content:
It's a tradition to cook halva and eat it after someone dies (not just for soldiers). It's believed that the halva is eaten for the good of the deceased. And there are many different kinds of halva. My favourite is the milk halva. The ingredients are similar to the one you've shown but it doesn't have the syrup and there is more milk, so the texture is very different. Then it's cooked in the oven (after the stirring part) until it has this nice little-burned (like caramelised) thin layer at top.

There's also lokma, which can be either sweet or salty, that's made and distributed to strangers for the charity of the deceased. People do it when someone they love dies. For example someone did it today for Ozzy Osbourne in Istanbul.

Author: @jkg6491
Content:
Whilst enjoyed all over Asia from India to Turkey, to even eastern Europe and Africa, Halwa has it's origins in Persia. 
Some also say it may have originated in Punjab (northwestern India and Pak) as that region has had sugar, wheat and dairy for thousands of years, as well as a history of producing other dairy, sugar and wheat based sweets (even teaching the Chinese the Art of making sugar from sugar cane). 

Also, originally, they add sugar right after the flour has browned a bit, and not in the form of syrup, so that it gives a more nutty flavour whilst getting caramelised, this method although more challenging yeilds more flavourful results. Water is added later in parts depending on how thick you want it. 

This method is still widely used in Persia and Punjab. But ofc people have their own methods and ingredients from place to place

Author: @UsernameAyse
Content: This is called "un helvası" in Turkiye, literally "flour halwa". If you have butter, flour, water and sugar, you can make it. If you use semolina instead, it's "irmik helvası" / semolina halwa. You can make it with or without milk, it softens both texture and taste. This isn't a desert you eat a full dish of - it is quite dense. Once you get the hang of it, you can add or reduce the sugar in the syrup to taste. Also, while there are so few ingredients, making this is a bit of a workout, and you need to be very careful not to burn yourself. The more brown you can get the butter-flour mixture without burning it, the better it will taste.

Author: @rajr1032
Content: Thanks, Max for letting us on the secrets of the heritage Turkish version of this confectionery / dessert, '-widely spread throughout the Middle East and North Africa, Eastern Europe and the Balkans, Central Asia, and South Asia-' (Wiki'). Here in India, the template is the north-Indian origin 'halwa' with a semolina base. Variations of this occasionally use wheat flour (whole flour, or alternatively, all-purpose flour), chickpea flour, fruit pulp and so on, as diverse as the country itself! Almost all the recipes, in its 'premier' version, calls for generous amounts of ghee ('clarified butter') and mixed nuts (cashew, almonds, pistachio). Wiki' also states that the word 'halva' entered the English language between 1840 and 1850. Here, it is spelt 'halwa', in the English of the British, our then colonial masters.

Author: @Historianchef
Content:
Thank you for this information. 😊 As a content creator focused on Turkish culinary history, I truly appreciate deep research in gastronomic heritage it’s essential for preserving and sharing cultural identity. 

This dish is called Gaziler Helvası it has a deep historical meaning in Turkish culinary tradition. It was often prepared for soldiers returning from war or in memory of martyrs. What’s fascinating is that during the Ottoman period, similar halvahs were distributed at public commemorations and military ceremonies, especially in the Acemi Ocağı. The nutritional density of helva made it ideal for recovery and remembrance. Love seeing such cultural dishes getting the spotlight!
